title: Reciprocity can halve what a mechanical network can learn
authors: Thai-Son Vu, Hoang-Giang Nguyen, Quoc-Bao Nguyen, Sengaloun Keoalounxay, Bao-Viet Tran
abstract: Tunable mechanical networks are being developed as materials that learn in place. Capacity is estimated by counting tunable parameters against target constraints, ignoring Maxwell-Betti reciprocity, the symmetry every passive, linear elastic network obeys by construction. When p degrees of freedom are both driven and read out, every reachable response block lies in a subspace of codimension p(p-1)/2, whatever the size, topology and stiffnesses; at full overlap nearly half the target space is unreachable. The consequence for training is a number: any learning rule leaves an error at least the norm of the target's antisymmetric part on the shared degrees of freedom, computable before training, and positive definiteness adds an orthogonal second term. A second-order optimiser with the exact Jacobian reaches that floor within 1% in 143 of 144 runs, a bond-local contrastive rule within 0.1% in 22 of 24, and odd couplings restore the lost directions at the price of an external torque source: the network becomes active. Prescribed-displacement drives obey a companion law we prove. The symmetry is classical; its consequence on a fixed graph with finitely many tunable stiffnesses at partial overlap is new. For a published robotic metamaterial it shows that no symmetric positive-definite stiffness matrix meets both targets in the linear model their deposited data integrate.
summary: This work analyzes the fundamental limits of learning in tunable mechanical networks by incorporating Maxwell-Betti reciprocity. It proves that this physical symmetry restricts the network's reachable response space, creating a quantifiable error floor that no passive training rule can overcome. The findings are crucial for designing physical machine learning hardware by setting realistic performance expectations.
main_problem: The paper determines the true capacity of tunable mechanical networks by accounting for physical symmetries, specifically Maxwell-Betti reciprocity, which constrains the reachable response space.
main_result: Reciprocity forces the reachable set into a subspace of codimension $p(p-1)/2$, establishing a computable error floor that limits the learning capability of passive networks.
method: The authors derive theoretical bounds using linear algebra and analyze the system's response block using the Jacobian, comparing theoretical constraints with numerical simulation results.
model_or_system: The system is a passive, linear elastic mechanical network with tunable stiffnesses, modeled by a bond force law. The analysis focuses on the response block $R(	heta)$ derived from the compliance matrix.
key_observables: The codimension of the reachable set, the error floor (related to the antisymmetric part of the target), and the rank of the Jacobian matrix.
important_parameters: The overlap $p$ (degrees of freedom both driven and read out), the number of bonds, and the stiffness parameters $	heta$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a fixed graph with a finite set of tunable stiffnesses, and the core results rely on the validity of Maxwell-Betti reciprocity for passive systems.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mechanical setup, showing how reciprocity constrains the response block to a lower-dimensional subspace, quantified by $p(p-1)/2$ lost dimensions.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model, derives the theoretical constraint imposed by reciprocity, calculates the resulting error floor, and then tests these theoretical limits using numerical simulations and optimization routines.
why_interesting: The concept of an inherent, physically imposed error floor in a learning system, derived from fundamental symmetries like reciprocity, provides a powerful theoretical constraint applicable to any physical realization of a neural network.

Forces are applied on a set S of degrees of freedom and displacements read on a set T; p = |T ∩S| of them are both driven and read out. (b) The bond force law. A passive bond pushes along its own axis and makes K symmetric; an odd bond adds a transverse component abˆtb and makes it asymmetric. (c) The response block C[T,S]. Maxwell–Betti forces its p× p sub-block on the shared degrees of freedom to be symmetric, which is p(p−1)/2 independent equalities and, by Theorem 1, p(p−1)/2 lost dimensions.
